#8846. How to Organize an Adaptive Triathlon for Kids (and Why It’ll Change Your Perspective)

Over 25 children participated in the adaptive Kids Tri for Champions event. (Photo: Courtesy Kevin Webb)

For this story, Triathlete spoke with the two organizers of the Kids Tri for Champions and one parent of a participant to understand what it takes to put on an adaptive triathlon for kids.

This whole swim-bike-run experience is supposed to be fun, but chasing PRs and podium finishes can make that easy to forget. If you’re overdue for a reminder, consider helping with an adaptive triathlon for kids.

An adaptive triathlon is not your typical race, and to find out why, as well as learn what it takes to successfully organize one, we spoke with Erik Wanberg, Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine student and the co-founder of Kids Tri for Champions: Adaptive Triathlon, and his co-organizer, Kevin Webb.

In 2024, Wanberg and several other Mayo Clinic medical students founded the first annual Kids Tri for Champions, an adaptive triathlon for children with developmental, intellectual, or physical special needs in grades kindergarten through 12th.

The race was part of the students’ second year of medical school, during which they’re provided with a variety of volunteer opportunities that they can receive school credit for. While they can choose to give back through existing community events and community service, Wanberg and the other students decided to create a new event, bringing their own interest in triathlon to children with disabilities when they realized the sport was inaccessible to them.

Nearly a dozen participants of all ability levels swam, biked, and ran their way to the finish line of the inclusive event at Soldier’s Field Park in Rochester, Minnesota.

“We started this race in an effort to fill an equity gap for children with disabilities in Southern Minnesota,” Wanberg says. “There are excellent resources here for adaptive physical education in our schools and fun after-school activities in our communities, but no real chance for the kids to participate in an actual competition that allows them to have that community race experience.”

Nearly one in five children in Minnesota and 3 million children across the U.S. live with a special health need or impairment. What’s more, physical activity levels are 4.5 times lower for disabled children. And for 1.5 million public primary and secondary school students with a physical disability, athletic competitions remain inaccessible.

“So we set out to create the first adaptive triathlon in this region where kids on the entire spectrum of intellectual and physical disabilities could swim, bike, and run,” Wanberg explains. Rather than emphasize competition, the Kids Tri for Champions focuses on inclusive recreation and self-achievement.

Now in its third year, the triathlon was held on July 11. Webb estimates that over 25 children between the ages of 4 and 18 years old participated.

“Over the past few years, our adaptive triathlon has accommodated children with capabilities ranging from Down syndrome to physical disabilities,” Webb says, “including hearing-impaired athletes and wheelchair users.”

“Adaptive events allow all kids to feel a strong sense of accomplishment,” says Anna Strand, whose daughter Ella is a Kids Tri for Champions’ finisher. “It gives them a chance to connect with friends and to work through a challenge in a way that raises their heart rate and also exposes them to a whole community that is supporting them and cheering them on.”

Inspired to offer an adaptive triathlon for children in your own community? Wanberg and Webb have some invaluable tips for organizing an inclusive event that is fun and safe for kids of all abilities.

1. Do set a date and a rain date, especially if your event will take place during thunderstorm season.

2. Do start planning early. For the Kids Tri for Champions in July, planning usually begins in January or February. Wanberg suggests sending out a Google form/survey that includes a direct question about each participant’s functional/ability level and event needs, including any specific accommodations that they will require during the event, such as an adaptive bike. The form should also include a section where participants can request that an athlete buddy partner with them for the entire race if they don’t want to bring their own. For Kids Tri for Champions, a link to the form is included in a promotional PDF for the event, which sponsors and supporters share on their websites and social media accounts.

3. Do establish a financial support system once you have a sense of how many participants to expect. Webb estimates that the Kids Tri for Champions costs about $400 to $500 annually for finisher medals, shirts, juice, and snacks, most of which is covered by donations from local nonprofits.

4. Do find a pool for the swim and plan your course around that. Kids Tri for Champions books the Soldier’s Field lap pool through Rochester Parks & Recreation, which provides a few lifeguards as well.

5. Do make sure that the course is in a contained environment that is publicly available, legal for the race, and straightforward. Wanberg suggests walking the course you’re considering to ensure there are no bumps, craters, or cracks that might make it hard or unsafe for adaptive bikes or individuals with poor balance.

6. Do put a team of volunteers together. Webb starts by emailing Mayo Clinic medical students.

“We get about 10 medical students, as well as people from the nonprofits We Bike Rochester and EA Therapeutic Health for a total of around 25 volunteers,” Webb says.

7. Do get help borrowing adaptive bikes (which can otherwise be expensive) by building a relationship with a local bike company or non-profit that can help with e-bikes, handcycles, tandems, recumbents, and upright bikes with training wheels. For the Kids Tri for Champions, EA Therapeutic Health brings a trailer of their physical therapy bikes to the race.

8. Do assign a buddy to swim with the athlete and run alongside them while they bike and run if it’s requested in the survey.

“Make sure that a couple of the buddies you recruit can run fast,” Webb advises. “Two years ago, a kid with an electric bike requested a buddy, so I ran with him, but he was doing 5:30 miles! So the next year, I recruited a couple high school cross-country runners just in case we had anyone on a fast bike.”

9. Do be flexible while putting safety first! Some of your participants may not be swimmers, which is why it’s crucial to have lifeguards on duty and floaties available. Have helmets available and insist that every athlete wear one while cycling.

“On race morning, mark the course, put out cones, and position volunteers at key points to keep athletes on the right path, but be ready to let them do their own thing, as long as it’s legal and safe,” Webb says. “One year, we marked the course to go clockwise, but the kid who finished the swim first began biking the other way and that’s what everybody else did. So we went counter-clockwise that day. It’s organized chaos and you have to embrace it.”

1. Don’t charge money. Keep the event free for families to offer a truly accessible triathlon.

2. Don’t limit the event to participants based on their abilities. Tailor the course to children with special needs but realize that part of what makes an adaptive triathlon so memorable for them is the opportunity to participate in an event with their siblings and peers of all abilities.

“This year there were two kids that were just planning on going to the pool that day,” Webb says. “They saw the triathlon and wanted to participate even though they hadn’t signed up, so we let them. That experience exposed them to people who have abilities that are different from their own, which is so cool!”

3. Don’t have a set distance … or order. Start the race in the pool but leave it up to each child to decide how far they feel comfortable swimming, whether that’s one lap or several. When the participant finishes swimming, their buddy can help them transition to the bike.

“In our triathlon, the kids bike on a trail around the pool, and their buddy runs alongside them,” Webb says. “What’s important is that each kid has a buddy with them and can choose for themselves if they want to bike or run a couple laps or turn around.”

4. Don’t underestimate the flexibility needed.

“There will be kids with varying intellectual and physical disabilities,” Wanberg says. “As such, there will be unforeseen obstacles on race day. Be ready to change things on the fly, typically at an individual participant level, if necessary to keep the race safe and fun.”

“We’ve had kids that swim, bike one lap, and jump back in the water instead of running,” Webb says. “Two years ago, I was a buddy for an athlete with Down syndrome who was maybe 10 years old. We were running along the trail and passed a public group doing yoga. He decided that he wanted to join them and the group was cool with it, so we took a yoga break.”

5. Don’t forget how much of an impact an adaptive triathlon can have on the kids – and you!

“Ella ran hard and she was tired, but seeing people cheer for her put a smile on her face,” Strand says. “The most meaningful part was seeing her sense of accomplishment as she finished the race!”

A few years ago, Webb remembers there was a teen at the finish line when he saw his friend starting the run. He just turned around and went with the other kid.

“It’s the opposite of the races I participate in, where it’s all about being competitive,” says Webb, who was part of the University of California, Davis’ Triathlon Club and now competes in trail races. “An adaptive kids triathlon is all about giving these children a sense of belonging in our communities. No matter what their pace or how far they go, I guarantee that they’re having more fun than we do at our races. It’s an awesome reminder to not take being able to run, bike, or swim for granted. It can reframe your perspective on sport.”

#8845. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

#8843. Latin America in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Social Housing, and Heritage Recovery

This October, architecture across Latin America became a platform for exchange, bringing together discussions on inhabitation, cultural identity, emerging practices, and the relationship between the built environment and its wider context. From conversations on emerging architectural practices and material research at Design Week Mexico to new approaches to housing, landscape, and public space in Chile and Mexico, recent developments highlight how architecture responds to specific local conditions. Across the region, initiatives addressing climate adaptation and heritage recovery in the Dominican Republic and Colombia also bring attention to the changing responsibilities of cultural institutions and the built environment.

Architecture as a Platform for Exchange: Biennials, Design, and Emerging Practices Across Latin America

The 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial brought architecture into a broader conversation about inhabitation, examining how social, cultural, environmental, and political conditions shape the ways people live. Held under the curatorial theme INHABIT, the event brought together international lectures, exhibitions, and public activities across six main venues and partner institutions, with contributions from architects including Smiljan Radić, Solano Benitez, Andrés Jaque, and Marina Otero Verzier. Through discussions on memory, materiality, urban development, and the relationship between architecture and its context, the Biennial positioned inhabitation as a framework for understanding architecture's role in shaping contemporary societies. Its exhibitions and public program continued throughout October as part of Buenos Aires Design and Architecture Month, extending the exchange beyond the International Forum and into the city's cultural institutions.

The event also provided the setting for ArchDaily's Next Practices Live in Mexico, hosted at Design House during the opening week of Design Week Mexico. Moderated by ArchDaily Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk, the conversation brought together 2026 Next Practices Awards winners MANUFACTURA, RAMA Estudio, and SOCA, alongside previous Mexican winners ASPJ and Palma, to discuss how emerging practices are expanding architecture's agency through material research, ecological knowledge, cultural engagement, and responses to specific social and environmental conditions.

Santa Rosa Social Housing / FAR frohn&rojas

Located along Avenida Santa Rosa in central Santiago, Santa Rosa Social Housing by FAR frohn&rojas explores an alternative approach to social housing by integrating residential units into the city's existing transportation and social infrastructure. Completed in 2026, the 2,337-square-meter project occupies an exceptionally narrow site, measuring less than nine meters wide, which informed the development of a seven-story building organized around a slender concrete structure. Most apartments are duplex units accessed through shared galleries, with living spaces opening onto circulation areas and bedrooms positioned on the upper levels. A perforated blue metal screen provides shading while preserving the expression of the raw concrete structure, and shared verandas introduce communal outdoor spaces. Developed through Chile's DS-49 social housing program, the project also incorporates a strategy to support the long-term maintenance of shared amenities through advertising revenue generated by its north-facing façade.

Located on the outskirts of Guadalajara, Mexico, Rancho del Abuelo by Mendiola Arregui is a 994-square-meter equestrian complex completed in 2026 that brings together facilities for horse care, recreation, and gathering within an existing landscape. The project is organized as a series of independent pavilions positioned in response to the site's existing conditions, with a shared architectural system connecting their different programs. Flat concrete roofs supported by columns establish a consistent structural framework, while independent walls define individual spaces and shape circulation, framing views of the landscape and surrounding trees. The separation between the roofs and walls allows natural light and ventilation to permeate the complex, creating a sequence of pathways, courtyards, and shaded areas.

Located along the Loncomilla River in San Javier de Loncomilla, Chile, Urban Mantle by Felipe Burgos Villablanca is a 16-square-meter public installation that seeks to reconnect the city with its riverfront and historical landscape. Developed as a contemplative seating structure, the project responds to the site's former role in colonial maritime trade and its gradual disconnection from the urban fabric. A curved concrete surface accommodates different resting positions, transforming an informal riverside gathering area into a space for rest, meditation, and landscape observation. Drawing on the work of Enric Miralles and Anne Holtrop, the design combines an organic form with a material approach that embraces the construction process and its imperfections.

Santo Domingo Tests UNESCO Climate Action Toolkit for Historic Heritage

The Colonial City of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic became the first cultural World Heritage property in Latin America and the Caribbean to pilot UNESCO's Climate Action Toolkit. Held from October 5 to 9, the workshop brought together heritage conservation, urban planning, and disaster risk management specialists to assess how hurricanes, heavy rainfall, and flooding could affect the historic center. Developed by UNESCO alongside ICCROM, ICOMOS, and IUCN, the toolkit connects climate projections and local knowledge with heritage management and planning strategies. The pilot will contribute to the development of a climate action plan for the historic district, highlighting the importance of integrating climate preparedness into the conservation of living urban heritage.

Colombia Mobilizes Cultural Institutions to Support Post-Earthquake Heritage Recovery

Following the August 10 earthquake, which affected cultural heritage across seven Colombian departments, several institutions launched initiatives in October to support recovery efforts. On October 6, the National Museum of Colombia, ICOM Colombia, and Universidad Externado de Colombia established a collection center in Bogotá to gather restoration materials for affected museums. The initiative followed reports of damage at 35 museums and museum institutions across 10 departments. Meanwhile, the District Institute of Cultural Heritage (IDPC) continued its volunteer program, carrying out architectural surveys, photographic documentation, and preliminary damage assessments in affected municipalities. These efforts form part of a broader recovery process led by cultural institutions and public authorities to assess damage, protect collections, and safeguard the country's architectural heritage.

#8842. Jan Frodeno and Flora Duffy on Olympic Gold vs. Ironman Paydays

This roundtable conversation, facilitated by Triathlete contributor Jordan Blanco, explores the push and pull professional triathletes feel when it comes to deciding whether to pursue the Olympics or other race series for financial gain.

We are two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, and short-course triathletes are approaching a decision that is both deeply personal and increasingly difficult to justify on a spreadsheet.

That tension was clearly on display at the recent Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii. Taylor Knibb added an Ironman world title to her palmares, even as the American is collecting Olympic qualifying points in the hope of racing a third Olympics on home soil in Los Angeles. Vincent Luis, a three-time Olympian and two-time short-course world champion, won Kona on his debut, having spent much of his career chasing Olympic success before making a late transition to long-course racing.

Others also offered different perspectives. Marten Van Riel described having been stuck in the Olympic pipeline for a long time before finally getting the opportunity to race in Kona. Ironman Hawaii third-place finisher and Olympic silver medalist from Paris 2024, Julie Derron, has not ruled out a return to short-course racing and a place on the Swiss Olympic team in 2028.

Their experiences reflect the choices of a growing number of professional triathletes. An Olympic campaign can consume an athlete’s schedule for years. Qualification requires global travel, points chasing, federation politics, and enough patience to build multiple seasons around a race that offers only three medals and no conventional prize purse. At the same time, T100 and the Ironman Pro Series circuit offer credible alternatives: more races, more ways to earn significant sums of money, and for some athletes, a clearer pathway to build a career in professional triathlon.

Yet reducing the choice to money misses much of what gives the Olympics their power. Jan Frodeno and Flora Duffy built two of the most decorated careers in triathlon, moving between the Olympic and long-course worlds in very different ways. Frodeno’s victory at the 2008 Beijing Games was the first race he had ever won. He later became a multiple Ironman and Ironman 70.3 world champion but remained known far beyond triathlon first as an Olympic champion. Duffy competed at five Games, won gold in Tokyo, and became a national figure in Bermuda. Even after exploring longer-distance racing, the Olympics remained her north star.

Their experiences also complicate the idea that athletes must choose between Olympic meaning and financial reward. Both describe the Olympic title as commercially valuable, although not in the form of race-day prize money. For Duffy, contracts tied to success in Tokyo and the new sponsors she signed afterward made Olympic gold financially lucrative. For Frodeno, being an Olympic Champion is a credential that continues to open doors almost two decades later.

But neither describes gold as an uncomplicated ending. Frodeno found himself struggling for direction after reaching the apparent summit of the sport in his first victory. Duffy returned for another quad because the possibility of repeating victory remained more compelling than a run at Kona.

Triathlete spoke with Frodeno and Duffy separately, then brought their answers together. The conversations have been condensed and edited for clarity.

Jan Frodeno: I come from not just a non-sporting but almost anti-sporting family. My parents had nothing to do with sports, and the only time sport was really valued was when the Olympics were on television. I remember being at my grandparents’ house during the 1988 Olympics. For two and a half weeks, the television was on nonstop, and the athletes who came home were cherished as heroes.

That planted a seed somewhere deep in my subconscious. I was always active and always needed an outlet, but sport wasn’t appreciated in my family at that time. The Olympics gave me a horizon – hope that I could change my stars. It was such an audacious goal that nobody really understood what it meant or could tell me it was completely crazy. It seemed like a parallel world where different people lived.

[The Olympics] gave me meaning and hope for close to two decades, until I actually got there. Triathlon wasn’t even in the Olympics in 1988. Later I met Conrad Stoltz, who went to Sydney for South Africa, and he was my first real Olympic contact. He was just a regular guy who happened to be better at triathlon than other people. Seeing that made the Olympics accessible. It made me realize I wanted to pursue that dream.

Flora Duffy: The Olympics were always the ultimate goal. They were what I dreamed of doing. I saw the Games as the pinnacle of sport when I was growing up. Every four years, I would sit down and watch, and the Olympics would take over.

Sydney was the first Games I clearly remember watching. There was something special about it. The event is iconic, everybody knows about it and it has such a rich history. Maybe part of it is that it happens only every four years. There is scarcity value. The buildup starts years in advance – just as we’re already talking about Los Angeles now.

Duffy: My position is probably different from that of many athletes because I come from such a small place. Bermuda sends an extremely small team to the Olympics: 10 athletes would be a lot. In Tokyo, there were only two of us.

Tyler Butterfield was a few years older than me and raced in Athens. He was the first Bermudian Olympian I could really relate to. He did triathlon, I did triathlon, and he was competing at the Olympic Games. Suddenly I could think, “Maybe I can do that too.” He had also competed at the Junior World Championships and won a medal before I did. Those moments made the pathway feel real.

I later saw what an Olympic medal could do for a small country, and I got to live the biggest version of that by winning gold in Tokyo. It meant so much. It united the island and became this deep, meaningful moment that transcended swim, bike, and run. There are now landmarks in Bermuda associated with me: the track at the national stadium, a pool at my high school, a road, murals. That shows how powerful the Olympics can be.

Frodeno: You go to the Olympics as a national athlete and contribute to your country’s medal table, but you also walk away with the honor yourself. [Being an Olympic champion] is forever, and it doesn’t really matter where you are from. It is the one title that sticks outside the triathlon bubble.

Hawaii is the Wimbledon of our sport. We care very deeply about it, and it is extremely meaningful to me. But when I make a public appearance, I am still introduced as the Olympic champion. That title shines beyond any individual sport.

There is also the experience of going as part of a national team. Triathlon is such an individual sport, but at the Olympics you live with athletes from completely different sports and share the experience with them. One of my roommates in Beijing was Moritz Fürste, the captain of the German hockey team. I won my medal a few days before the hockey team won theirs, and it was wild.

Frodeno: You get one shot every four years. A world championship happens every year – and that is not to take anything away from a world championship – but having one chance in four years exponentially increases the potential for error. Most athletes might get one or two Olympic opportunities in a career. A few get three. Flora went five times, which is crazy.

That scarcity gives it something special. It reaches beyond the sport itself. The title of Olympic champion stays with you in a way that almost nothing does.

Duffy: There are only three medals. If you finish fourth, fifth or sixth, there is no prize money. You leave empty-handed after dedicating the previous four years – or more – to that one event.

At the same time, that uncertainty is part of what makes sport beautiful. You never know what is going to happen on the day. That is why athletes train and pursue the goal. They build their whole careers around chasing that one opportunity.

Duffy: For most of my career, racing short course was quite lucrative. I loved the fast, dynamic style of racing, and I had enough success early on to stay committed to it. Each Olympic build was different, and I was a different athlete in every cycle, so I wasn’t looking around and asking what else I could do in triathlon.

Now there are many more opportunities. Athletes are trying to decide whether to race short-course, T100, or the Ironman Pro Series while also attempting to qualify for the Olympics. The danger is they spread themselves too thin.

Are you pursuing the Olympics because that is your dream and your ultimate goal? Or do you want to focus on T100 and the Ironman Pro Series because you want to make money? For some athletes, that is the goal. They are not interested in the Olympics, and there is nothing wrong with that.

The other side is that short-course athletes may receive federation funding, health insurance, and travel support. They might not be earning a huge amount, but they have enough security to pursue the goal without relying entirely on sponsors or race results. The calculation is more complicated than looking only at prize purses.

Frodeno: I don’t know that I would have chosen differently. Don’t get me wrong: I am definitely economically motivated. But there were lucrative races in my era too. Hy-Vee put enormous money on the line, and I never really chased it.

I think it is fantastic that athletes now have so many possibilities. But more choice can also make the decision harder. Going through a federation can be frustrating and grating because volunteers are sometimes making the decisions that affect your professional career. It can look easier to get a pro license and pursue immediate prize money.

Still, if the Olympics are what genuinely pull you, that experience is not something you can recreate later. It is not something you can read about in a blog after the fact.

Duffy: Standing on an Olympic podium with a medal around your neck is priceless, but it can also lead to more sponsorship and exposure. My situation was unique because my contracts were geared toward Tokyo and winning there. For me, it was a very lucrative day. I also signed new sponsors afterward because I was the Olympic champion.

That success carried into the next cycle. A lot of my sponsors were geared toward Paris and short-course racing, so they were happy that I remained on that path. There was also all this momentum around returning to the Olympics as the defending champion, particularly as someone from a small island.

Frodeno: It changed my circumstances, but the lasting commercial value was not simply cashing in on the medal or earning a certain amount in sponsorship. That fades relatively quickly. The unique thing about being an Olympic champion is that it is a door opener.

That is still valued commercially now, 18 years later. I don’t walk around with my medal. It is more something that people say about you than something you need to say about yourself. But the title carries.

Frodeno: What many people don’t realize is that the Olympics were the first race I ever won. I had never won a World Cup. I went from never having tasted victory to reaching the apparent end state of the game on my first win.

That was wonderful, but it was also the pinnacle. Any World Cup afterward could not compare to three helicopters overhead, the media coverage, and the scale of the Olympics. It also threw me into some of the darkest times of my life because I struggled to find meaning afterward. It was seven years before I won my first world title, at the 2015 70.3 World Championship, and during that period I wondered whether I was a one-hit wonder.

I had thought winning gold would mean arriving at all my dreams. It took me from a miserable little apartment to a wonderful loft, a fancy car, and flying business class. But I didn’t see the writing on the wall soon enough that what I actually loved about triathlon was triathlon itself and the training. It was – and still is – just a love for the sport.

A few weeks before Beijing, I remember completing a brutal session in the rain and telling myself, “If you get through this, you never have to go this hard again.” In hindsight, that was strange, because hard training was what I chose to keep doing for nearly two more decades.

Duffy: Tokyo was hugely meaningful for me, my team and my country. Going into Paris, the intrigue was whether I could do it again. Could I win another medal? Could I defend the title and become a two-time Olympic champion?

The Olympics had always been my ultimate goal. Even late in my career, I never developed the dream of going to Kona and winning. I thought that bug would catch me but it never did.

Now that I am retired, if I ask myself whether I wish I had a proper shot at Kona or a better build into Paris, my regret is that I did not have a better build into Paris. I don’t regret not racing Kona. That says a lot about where the Olympics sat for me.

Frodeno: I went to two Olympics, but I did not have the guts to recognize that my Olympic ambition and campaign were effectively done by 2012. I loved the experience, but I probably should have gone a different way after Beijing. As John Mayer sings in Gravity, “Twice as much is not twice as good.”

It is difficult to give generic advice because everybody comes from a different place. The thing I did well was to listen to my gut. My mother wanted me to study because she was looking after my best interests, but I knew I had to go all in. At the time, almost nobody was making money in Olympic-distance triathlon, but I followed what I enjoyed most and found a way to build a career around it.

Duffy: For many, the Olympic pathway comes first, and then, assuming they remain healthy, they move to middle- or long-distance racing later. They have their Olympic experience, whether it was good, disappointing or successful, and then they begin the second part of their career.

My path was different because the Olympic goal continued to excite me. The possibility of returning for Paris meant more to me than moving fully into long-course racing. That will not be true for every athlete, and it should not be.

This is a hard lifestyle. What is going to get you out of bed to train for several hours a day and deal with injuries? The answer is different for everybody. For me, it was the Olympics.

Duffy: Athletes often go into the Olympics with slightly unrealistic expectations. On one hand, that is good. You have to dream and believe. But if you are not realistic, you can come out the other side deeply disappointed.

Everything is heightened at the Olympics: the pressure, expectations and noise. The buildup is stressful. There is team selection, chasing points around the world, dealing with injuries and trying to arrive at the last minute in the right shape. It is extremely difficult, but it is also extremely rewarding.

Unrealistic expectations can take some of the joy out of racing at an iconic venue and representing your country. I was guilty of that in Paris. It was my fifth and final Olympics, and I already had a gold medal. The result was not going to make or break my career. But I finished fifth and was extremely disappointed, and that disappointment took away some of the joy of being at the Games and watching athletes from around the world.

It is difficult to balance expectations with appreciating the moment. Athletes should dream big, but they should also understand how hard it is to perform on that one day.

Frodeno: Nowadays, the decision is probably harder because there is so much choice. The one thing I did well was listen to my gut instinct. If the Olympics really get to you – particularly with a home Games in Los Angeles – riding through the streets of LA with tens of thousands, hopefully hundreds of thousands of people cheering is priceless. It is not an economic choice. It is about living life to the fullest.

Experiencing the Olympics through your national team and alongside athletes from other sports is a unique construct. It brings a core group of people together in a way that money cannot buy.

#8841. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#8838. 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s important to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically shows up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

Last medically reviewed on February 12, 2025

#8836. DMA, Nasher and Modern Art Museum Fort Worth Directors in Conversation

Program Overview:As North Texas continues to grow, its cultural landscape is evolving as well. In addition to meeting the needs of a new generation of North Texans, the museums of Dallas and Fort Worth are welcoming new directors who are ushering in a different kind of museum visitor, one who sees the world through a rapidly shifting cultural lens and, perhaps, through a reconsidered architectural lens as well. Whether leading a capital building project or rethinking what it means to engage with a museum collection in a revered space, this panel discussion will explore insights from the three newest museum directors in North Texas and how their perspectives are shaping the arts and experiences of 21st-century museum visitors. Moderated by Kate Aoki, AIA, NOMA of Golden Egg Creative, our Panelists are Carlos Basualdo, Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center, Brian Ferriso, Director of the Dallas Museum of Art, and Halona NORTON WESTBROOK, PhD, Director of the Modern Art Museum Fort Worth in this intriguing, enlightening and unique program. Free, open to the public, no reservations needed.Program Participants:Carlos Basualdo is the Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center. From 2022 to 2025, Basualdo served as Marion Boulton (Kippy) Stroud Deputy Director and Chief Curator at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Some of his Philadelphia exhibitions include Bruce Nauman: Topological Gardens, which represented the United States at the 2009 Venice Biennale and received the Golden Lion for Best National Participation; Dancing Around the Bride; Barbara Chase-Riboud: The Malcolm X Series; and Jasper Johns: Mind/Mirror. He has also curated Tropicália: A Revolution in Brazilian Culture and served as a co-curator of Documenta11 and a member of the curatorial team of the 50th Venice Biennale, where he organized The Structure of Survival. Basualdo has held curatorial positions at MAXXI in Rome and the Wexner Center for the Arts and has taught at IUAV University of Venice and Penn Design at the University of Pennsylvania. He was a 2013 Fellow of the Center for Curatorial Leadership in New York City. As Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center, he oversees one of the finest collections of modern and contemporary sculptures in the world, the Raymond and Patsy Nasher Collection, featuring more than 300 masterpieces by Calder, de Kooning, di Suvero, Giacometti, Hepworth, Kelly, Matisse, Miró, Moore, Picasso, Rodin, Serra and more. The Nasher Sculpture Center presents rotating exhibitions of works from the Nasher family collection as well as special exhibitions drawn from other museums and private collections. The Center also presents The Nasher Prize, an award dedicated to excellence in contemporary sculpture, honoring a living artist whose work has had an extraordinary impact on the medium.Brian Ferriso is The Eugene McDermott Director of the Dallas Museum of Art, a role he assumed in December 2025 after nearly two decades as Director of the Portland Art Museum (PAM). With almost 30 years of museum leadership experience, Ferriso has demonstrated success in advancing ambitious capital projects, strengthening collections, and expanding community access. During his tenure, he more than doubled the museum's curatorial staff and increased the endowment by $40 million Under his leadership, PAM served as the co-presenting institution for the space in which to place me (2024), Jeffrey Gibson's exhibition for the U.S. Pavilion at the Venice Biennale—the first solo presentation by an Indigenous artist for the U.S. Pavilion. Ferriso also oversaw a $140 million campus expansion, which added nearly 100,000 square feet of public and gallery space to the PAM campus. He championed acquisitions by women and artists of color and expanded Native American representation in the museum's collection and leadership. Prior to his role at PAM, Ferriso was the Executive Director and CEO of the Philbrook Museum of Art, and earlier in his career, he held leadership roles at the Milwaukee Art Museum and the Smart Museum of Art at the University of Chicago. He holds a bachelor's degree in economics from Bowdoin College, a master's degree in arts administration from New York University, and a master's degree in art history from the University of Chicago. The DMA is an inclusive, welcoming space for everyone to see its global collection of more than 25,000 works spanning 5,000 years of history and a range of world cultures. It is one of the largest art museums in the United States. The DMA provides educational programming for all ages, from exhibitions and lectures to concerts, literary events, and dramatic performances. Under Ferriso's leadership, the DMA is advancing a transformative building project that will reimagine the Museum's campus, enhance the visitor experience, and strengthen its connection to the surrounding Arts District. The project represents a significant investment in the DMA's future, positioning the Museum to better serve its growing audiences and the Dallas community for generations to come.Halona Norton-Westbrook, Ph.D., began her tenure as Director of the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth in July 2025. She served as the Director and CEO of the Honolulu Museum of Art from 2020–25, and prior to that was Director of Curatorial Affairs and Curator of Modern and Contemporary Art at the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio. Norton-Westbrook is a visionary museum leader with a proven track record of institutional transformation and audience expansion. At the Honolulu Museum of Art, she doubled annual attendance from pre-2020 levels, secured millions of dollars in gifts to the museum's endowment and significantly expanded the institution's fundraising efforts. Managing a staff of 150 employees, she led the museum through a successful American Alliance of Museums reaccreditation, developed its first comprehensive strategic plan, and guided a restoration and expansion of its historic art school. Norton-Westbrook is a passionate advocate for museums and the vital role that they play in providing access to the arts, fostering greater empathy, connection, and creativity in the lives of individuals and communities as a whole. She has extensive expertise in modern and contemporary art as well as the formation, history, and evolution of museum collections in the twentieth century. Raised in the San Francisco Bay area, Norton-Westbrook earned a BA in American History and Studio Art from Mills College in Oakland, California, an MA in Art History from Courtauld Institute of Art in London, and a Ph.D. in Museology from the University of Manchester.Moderator: Kate Aoki, AIA, NOMA, is an architect and founding partner of experience and exhibition design firm Golden Egg Creative. With degrees in textile design and architecture, Kate is fortunate to practice in a profession that satisfies both her passion for fine art and the design of space. After spending more than a decade working in the architecture field, Kate shifted to a position as the Head of Exhibition Design at the Dallas Museum of Art where she developed a deeper appreciation for inclusion and public spaces. As Director of Design for Golden Egg Creative, Kate designs connective spaces in ways that engage visitors while inviting them to learn more about objects they experience and the communities in which they thrive.Kate has dedicated much of her time to participating on art and architectural committees as well as teaching design studios as an adjunct professor for architecture at the University of Texas at Arlington's CAPPA. She has a longstanding relationship with the Dallas chapter of the AIA, where she served as President in 2023, and the Texas Society of Architects as a member of the Government Affairs Steering Committee. Kate is a member of the Board of Directors of The Dallas Architecture Forum, where she founded the Design Society. Now as a resident of Santa Fe, New Mexico, Kate is excited to be learning more about the rich cultural history and practices of the Southwest.

Program Overview:As North Texas continues to grow, its cultural landscape is evolving as well. In addition to meeting the needs of a new generation of North Texans, the museums of Dallas and Fort Worth are welcoming new directors who are ushering in a different kind of museum visitor, one who sees the world through a rapidly shifting cultural lens and, perhaps, through a reconsidered architectural lens as well. Whether leading a capital building project or rethinking what it means to engage with a museum collection in a revered space, this panel discussion will explore insights from the three newest museum directors in North Texas and how their perspectives are shaping the arts and experiences of 21st-century museum visitors. Moderated by Kate Aoki, AIA, NOMA of Golden Egg Creative, our Panelists are Carlos Basualdo, Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center, Brian Ferriso, Director of the Dallas Museum of Art, and Halona NORTON WESTBROOK, PhD, Director of the Modern Art Museum Fort Worth in this intriguing, enlightening and unique program. Free, open to the public, no reservations needed.Program Participants:Carlos Basualdo is the Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center. From 2022 to 2025, Basualdo served as Marion Boulton (Kippy) Stroud Deputy Director and Chief Curator at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Some of his Philadelphia exhibitions include Bruce Nauman: Topological Gardens, which represented the United States at the 2009 Venice Biennale and received the Golden Lion for Best National Participation; Dancing Around the Bride; Barbara Chase-Riboud: The Malcolm X Series; and Jasper Johns: Mind/Mirror. He has also curated Tropicália: A Revolution in Brazilian Culture and served as a co-curator of Documenta11 and a member of the curatorial team of the 50th Venice Biennale, where he organized The Structure of Survival. Basualdo has held curatorial positions at MAXXI in Rome and the Wexner Center for the Arts and has taught at IUAV University of Venice and Penn Design at the University of Pennsylvania. He was a 2013 Fellow of the Center for Curatorial Leadership in New York City. As Director of the Nasher Sculpture Center, he oversees one of the finest collections of modern and contemporary sculptures in the world, the Raymond and Patsy Nasher Collection, featuring more than 300 masterpieces by Calder, de Kooning, di Suvero, Giacometti, Hepworth, Kelly, Matisse, Miró, Moore, Picasso, Rodin, Serra and more. The Nasher Sculpture Center presents rotating exhibitions of works from the Nasher family collection as well as special exhibitions drawn from other museums and private collections. The Center also presents The Nasher Prize, an award dedicated to excellence in contemporary sculpture, honoring a living artist whose work has had an extraordinary impact on the medium.Brian Ferriso is The Eugene McDermott Director of the Dallas Museum of Art, a role he assumed in December 2025 after nearly two decades as Director of the Portland Art Museum (PAM). With almost 30 years of museum leadership experience, Ferriso has demonstrated success in advancing ambitious capital projects, strengthening collections, and expanding community access. During his tenure, he more than doubled the museum's curatorial staff and increased the endowment by $40 million Under his leadership, PAM served as the co-presenting institution for the space in which to place me (2024), Jeffrey Gibson's exhibition for the U.S. Pavilion at the Venice Biennale—the first solo presentation by an Indigenous artist for the U.S. Pavilion. Ferriso also oversaw a $140 million campus expansion, which added nearly 100,000 square feet of public and gallery space to the PAM campus. He championed acquisitions by women and artists of color and expanded Native American representation in the museum's collection and leadership. Prior to his role at PAM, Ferriso was the Executive Director and CEO of the Philbrook Museum of Art, and earlier in his career, he held leadership roles at the Milwaukee Art Museum and the Smart Museum of Art at the University of Chicago. He holds a bachelor's degree in economics from Bowdoin College, a master's degree in arts administration from New York University, and a master's degree in art history from the University of Chicago. The DMA is an inclusive, welcoming space for everyone to see its global collection of more than 25,000 works spanning 5,000 years of history and a range of world cultures. It is one of the largest art museums in the United States. The DMA provides educational programming for all ages, from exhibitions and lectures to concerts, literary events, and dramatic performances. Under Ferriso's leadership, the DMA is advancing a transformative building project that will reimagine the Museum's campus, enhance the visitor experience, and strengthen its connection to the surrounding Arts District. #8835. 7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin issue.

So, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

Acne typically shows up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

By comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

Acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

One key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

An ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny new hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

Sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the issue. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It shows up as painful sores or blisters.

Since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

Other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment plan.

Last medically reviewed on February 14, 2025

It's normal to experience some skin issues from time to time. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign of something more serious.

Read the original version in Spanish here.

To say that we design "for people" seems like a fundamental premise of architecture. Yet, this assertion presents a problem: people are not a homogeneous category.

To say that we design "for people" seems like a fundamental premise of architecture. Yet, this assertion presents a problem: people are not a homogeneous category.

Human-Centered Design challenges us to question whom we observe, listen to, and represent when making design decisions. Through an interdisciplinary discussion, we will explore how physical, sensory, and social needs influence architecture and interior design, and how these factors shape the way we live, feel, and connect.

#8831. The Latest and Greatest Sunglasses for Triathletes, Tested in Training and Racing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Sunglasses and triathletes go hand in hand. With not one but two sports calling for a good pair, and after so much time spent nitpicking over the perfect goggles, we can’t settle for less when it comes to shading our eyes through the bulk of our training and racing.

It’s not just about UV protection and keeping bugs and debris out, because, let’s be honest: style matters, too. And today’s saturated performance sunglasses market offers a nearly unlimited selection of styles, with many pairs more high-tech and often higher-priced than ever before.

We wanted to get a clearer, less-tinted picture of the triathlon-worthy sunglasses landscape in 2026, so we combed the internet to see what was on the cutting edge and spent the summer testing a wide range of pairs while running and cycling across different terrains and climates.

Along the way, we explored the latest tech, picked out standout features, and figured out what felt worth the money – and what wasn’t quite there yet. From light-shifting photochromic lenses and video-recording AI smart glasses to everyday pairs that won’t break the bank, here’s our roundup of the best sunglasses for triathletes in 2026.

In the Pacific Northwest where I live, it can be raining one minute and sunny the next. A ride might take you from wide-open roads into dense, dark forests, sometimes around a single corner. For that reason, I’ve found light-shifting lenses incredibly useful. But even if you don’t live where I do, these glasses are practical in plenty of other changing light conditions, such as an early-morning long ride that starts before the sun comes up and ends well into the day.

One of the biggest drawbacks of traditional photochromic sunglasses is that the lenses don’t always adjust as quickly as the light changes. Their tint range also has limits, and they don’t always get as clear or as dark as you’d like. Most rely on UV light to darken, which means they may not respond as you’d expect behind a UV-blocking windshield in your car or when you’re testing them by a window before heading outside.

That’s a perfect segue into where we’ll start, as the first pair on our list looks to address these issues by taking a different approach: tint you control with a swipe.

One of the most intriguing pairs on this entire list comes from a new brand called Povec. Rather than waiting for the lenses to react to changing light, these glasses allow you to swipe an interface on the temple to change the tint in about a second.

Sure enough, I was surprised by just how quickly, and how dramatically, the tint changed. It started shifting as soon as we swiped the temple, so naturally, we spent the next several days playing with it back and forth. The electrochromic tech, as it’s called, worked so well that the glasses quickly became a showpiece for impressing friends.

These glasses ironically shone in dimmer conditions, especially when we went off-road or deep into the forests and needed to change the tint quickly. When mountain biking, being able to change the tint almost immediately as we rounded a corner into a dense forest descent felt invaluable.

At the same time, we were slightly less impressed with the optical quality in harsher light. There are subtle but apparent reflections, and the clarity is just a little off. It’s nothing dramatic, but it is noticeable, especially compared with the crystal-clear optics of some other glasses on this list.

Our favorite everyday pair of photochromic sunglasses, especially for spring and fall days in the PNW forests, was the SunGod Velans 2.

This ultralight pair offered some of the best optical clarity, field of view, and comfort of any glasses on this list, even before the added bonus of photochromic lenses. They shifted from light to dark quickly enough for our normal riding, although they couldn’t match the on-demand tint changes of the Povecs.

SunGod has become increasingly visible in triathlon thanks to athletes such as Hayden Wilde and Chelsea Sodaro donning them, but also because of a few appealing extras not often found elsewhere in the market. An array of customization options, an emphasis on durability, repairability, and recycled packaging, and a lifetime guarantee that includes repairs for accidental breakage make the higher price easier to digest. Furthermore, features such as replacement lenses and screwless hinges make the price more logical and suggest this pair will likely last you for the long term rather than just a couple of seasons.

Tifosi consistently makes it into our roundups for offering quality sunglasses at some of the best prices, and its light-shifting options are no exception.

We tried the Rail XC with Clarion Blue “Fototec” lenses, which offer a stated light-transmission range of 12% to 46%.

Compared with the SunGods, these felt like only a small step down in optical quality and fit during our testing. We did notice more glare from sunlight at certain angles and slightly more fogging during humid runs. At 31 grams, they were also a little heavier.

But beyond that, there’s little else to nitpick. They’re comfortable, clear, and transition smoothly and quickly, with nose pads and temple tips that adjust on the fly, offering plenty of room to dial in comfort.

Perhaps the most controversial pair on this list, these smart glasses have divided opinions about where this technology belongs in triathlon. From Ironman banning their use at its events to T100 welcoming them through a partnership, it’s a hot topic.

After training and racing in them twice, my own mixed opinion comes down to something simpler: I thoroughly enjoy wearing them and appreciate their practicality, but I’m still struggling with the bulky styling of the Vanguard. Enough so that I often intentionally leave them behind so I’m not the guy with the video sunglasses when running or cycling with friends.

That functionality, on the other hand, is hard to argue with. Being able to capture hands-free video and photos, listen to music, take phone calls, and ask Meta questions — among many other features — makes these glasses useful in ways a regular pair simply can’t match.

The Oakley Prizm lenses offered the clarity we expected, although the bulkier frame slightly restricted the field of view. Even after keeping them in their case and using only a microfiber cloth to clean them, I also noticed tiny scratches under close inspection after a few months of use. They weren’t noticeable while wearing the glasses, but they were there.

At 66 grams, you’ll notice the weight, too. If you have one of the lightweight alternatives on this list sitting next to them, you might think twice before grabbing these for an everyday session.

Where these really earned their place is in documenting your triathlon experiences. At SOS Triathlon and Escape from Alcatraz, capturing moments before, during, and after the race felt almost effortless. I could quickly tell Meta to take a photo or record a video, then download the footage to my phone through the app afterward, and I was set. Compared with previously having to bring GoPros, set up shots, and worry about batteries and SD cards, it makes it all too easy.

On the way to the SOS check-in tent, I even asked Meta to help me remember the different stages of this unique multi-stage race (read more about the SOS here).

Like it or not, smart glasses are likely to become an increasingly familiar sight around triathletes. After using them, I can understand the appeal.

Read a full Oakley Meta Vanguard review here.

The award for the most pleasantly surprising sunglasses on this entire list goes to this Oakley Meta rival, which packed in enough features to put the Vanguard on the ropes.

I’ll admit I went into testing the Rover sunglasses with the preconceived notion that these wouldn’t compete with the powerhouse name above. But I was taken aback by both the quality and functionality.

The first things I noticed were the weight, more than 10 grams lighter than the Vanguard, and the lenses. I hadn’t expected optics this good from a brand I had never heard of.

Then it only got better. The Rovers offer both landscape and portrait recording, plus a tiltable camera that helps you adjust the shot. The video resolution was also better than I expected at 3K and 60 fps – all capabilities the Vanguard doesn’t offer.

One of the standout features was the intercom function, which lets the glasses act like a walkie-talkie with fellow cyclists using the BleeqUp app. Being able to talk to each other more easily is something I’ve always wanted on small group rides, and hearing everyone clearly through the sunglasses themselves takes away the hassle of phone calls or dealing with headphones.

They’re marketed as AI sunglasses, with tools for quickly editing captured footage and adding ride-data overlays. If you’re feeling extra AI-adventurous, you can also generate a third-person view of your ride using mapping data and an uploaded photo of yourself and your bike. The results were interesting, to say the least.

Where the Rovers fell slightly behind the Vanguards was in the polish. The interface, AI assistant, and connectivity didn’t feel as refined as Meta’s. The feedback sounds weren’t as distinct, and connecting the glasses could be a little confusing, with frequent requests to reconnect to their Wi-Fi.

The Vanguard also comes with a charging case, which simplifies things, while the Rover uses a magnetic USB charger. Finally, having to say “Hey Bleeker” to activate the assistant just felt super weird.

One final gripe: The temples could rub against the lenses when folded, which felt like a small but frustrating design oversight.

In contrast to the pleasant surprise of the BleeqUp Rovers, these heads-up display sunglasses fell well short of my expectations.

I was excited to see whether technology similar to what we’ve enjoyed in Form’s smart swim goggles could bring the same benefit to running and cycling. Unfortunately, I was disappointed from the moment I unboxed them.

The idea is great, but the execution wasn’t there. The fit was the least comfortable of any glasses on this list, sitting unusually high on my face, and the secondary inner lens that houses the HUD projection compromised the view.

The bright green data displayed on the inner lenses is intended to keep cyclists from having to look down at their bike computer so they can focus on what’s ahead. In practice, however, I found the view even more distracting, sometimes struggling to adjust my focus from what I was reading on the glasses back to the road.

It was less of an issue while running, and thankfully, you can adjust the brightness and make some changes to the display position to keep the data less intrusive, but that was little consolation.

The app also felt unfinished, and we experienced several issues trying to connect our devices. Top it off with the worst-sounding built-in speakers and most robotic voice assistants I’ve heard in a while, and I’ll sadly be leaving HUD glasses out of my periphery for a while.

If I had the budget and could choose just one everyday pair to wear everyday or bring on a trip, like our recent all-in Ironman World Championship coverage, I’d choose the Oslo 2.0.

The blend of aesthetics, lens quality, and fit is hard to beat. Grippy temple tips and a very grippy nosepiece (which comes in various sizes) help it transition easily from casual use to training. Although it doesn’t look like it’s meant for running, it performs as well as a pair designed specifically for the sport.

For cycling, though, I prefer a little more lens coverage. That’s where I’d reach for Roka’s San Remo Air, which offers a similarly understated cafe style, but with more coverage and a vented lens for hot days.

Both were pairs I could happily wear all day, and all night if I had to. They also had some of the fewest fogging issues while running in the heat and humidity of a Washington summer and felt among the most premium of the bunch — from the finish of the frames to the cases they came in.

Our favorite mid-priced everyday pair was the Adidas Kaphiros, which came surprisingly close to the Rokas in overall performance. It also became the pair my wife consistently stole – sorry, “borrowed” – before we headed out for a ride together.

These are truly glasses you forget you’re wearing. They almost feel like they float above your ears. If pressure around your ears is something that regularly bothers you — as it has for me in the past — this is the pair I’d recommend.

The lenses offer generous coverage for cycling protection, and the optical quality impressed me. Small openings in the temples let air through while riding, although the glasses tended to fog during hot, humid runs — likely due to the size of the lenses.

Tifosi makes this list for a second time, beating out plenty of other running and cycling sunglasses as our favorite budget everyday pair.

The Vogel XC is lightweight, has proved durable enough to survive a couple of seasons with me, and offers a rimless, vented design that’s hard to beat at this price.

The lens tint we tested hit a useful middle ground for the varied conditions we wore it in. And the size and shape don’t scream “I’m a triathlete” every time you wear them out in public.
