Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

The math behind one of travel rewards' best-kept secrets

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#8829. 7 Places on the Body That Hidradenitis Suppurativa Can Appear

Despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body. We’re all prone to the occasional bump, rash, zit, or ingrown hair. These issues generally go away after the blocked follicle, clogged pore, or minor skin irritation resolves.

But hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different. HS is a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in some of your most sensitive regions (and beyond).

HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain. Although infections are often a part of HS, the disease itself is not an infection — it’s due to an ongoing inflammatory response in the body.

In addition to causing pain and discomfort, HS can be extremely frustrating and impact your self-esteem. Identifying HS correctly and early is crucial for getting optimal care, easing symptoms, slowing disease progression, and improving your mental health.

While we don’t know what exactly causes HS, genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors may play a role. Skin regions prone to HS include those where we sweat often and where friction is super common. Friction can occur from skin rubbing on skin, or where clothing can chafe or rub.

Here are seven areas of the body that are often impacted by HS.

Our underarms are packed with hair follicles and apocrine glands (aka, sweat glands). With HS, these follicles and glands may become clogged, and bacteria can start to grow, leading to the inflamed boil-like bumps of HS.

If you’ve ever gone for a run and come back with the dreaded armpit chafing, you’re all too familiar with how this area of the body can be prone to skin-on-skin friction or excessive rubbing from clothing. (Lookin’ at you, sports bra!) Friction and chafing can also cause an HS flare-up.

Complicating matters is that some people shave or wax their armpits, and many understandably slather this region with antiperspirants or deodorants. These factors can also clog or irritate sweat glands and hair follicles.

The breasts, including underneath and even on the areolae (the area around the nipple), are a common place for HS to show up.

The breast area is a frequent spot for chafing from bras or other clothing. This chafing not only causes skin irritation — it can also trap sweat and bacteria on the skin. The areolae contain apocrine glands and hair follicles that can easily become infected. All these factors can contribute to an HS flare.

Research also points to sex hormones playing a role in HS, so a hormone shift or imbalance may also make breast tissue more prone to HS lesions. However, more research is needed on the connection between HS and hormones.

No one can deny that the crotch becomes a sweaty area when life gets steamy, either from the weather, a workout, or both. It’s also a common area for clothing to rub against just from walking and everyday movements.

As with other HS-prone areas, the groin and genital areas contain apocrine glands and oodles of hair follicles, all of which can become blocked as part of HS, leading to a flare. Speaking of hair down there, many people groom their pubic region, which can also lead to blocked hair follicles.

Again, hormonal shifts or imbalances may also play a role in why these sensitive areas can become hot spots for HS.

The inner thighs are an extension of the groin area. Similarly, sweat also hangs out here, and it’s a common spot for chafing to occur from skin-on-skin friction, or from clothing rubbing and irritating the area.

The entire buttocks area is also prone to HS in many people. Areas commonly affected include the anus, the butt crack, and the gluteal fold — or the crease where the buttocks meet the backs of the upper thighs.

Apocrine glands and hair follicles are abundant here, too. Sweat and other bacteria sources can also lead to HS infections. The buttocks are also subjected to pressure from sitting, which can lead to further irritation.

Although more research is needed, some studies suggest a link between HS and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IBD is an umbrella term for conditions such as Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis. The potential links between HS and IBD may play a role in why the buttocks area is a common site for HS.

Although less common than in other areas, HS can also show up at the nape of the neck. This might be due to friction from clothing collars, jewelry, and other clothing or accessories. The neck is also a common site for sweat, which could block hair follicles in this area.

If skin folds at the waist, or clothing waistbands (especially tight ones!) cause friction, it can lead to HS in the waistband area. As a result, HS lesions may show up on the abdomen, back, or sides.

HS tends to appear on some of the body’s most sensitive places, including the underarms, breasts, groin, and buttocks. These areas are prone to sweat, friction, and irritation from hair removal — all of which may contribute to an HS flare.

If you suspect you have HS, talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can give you a proper diagnosis and help you develop the right treatment and self-care plan to combat irritation and flares so you can feel more comfortable in your skin.

Last medically reviewed on February 28, 2025

It's normal to experience some skin issues from time to time. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign of something more serious.

#8820. The Swedish Sport of Swimrun Is Spreading Across the U.S. I Tried It and Chaos Ensued.

Outside features editor Frederick Dreier participated in the October 4 Ötillö Swimrun race at Horsetooth Reservoir, Colorado. Dreier has competed in triathlons, bicycle races, and other endurance sports for 25 years.

A few memories come to mind from my recent Ötillö Swimrun, the endurance race that combines open-water swimming with trail running.

In one, I flounder in the chilly waters of Colorado’s Horsetooth Reservoir near Fort Collins, my arms feeling heavy as concrete as I struggle to swim in a straight line. In another, I sit by the side of a rocky trail plucking cactus spines out of my backside, moments after a clumsy toe-strike sent me tumbling into a clump of prickly pear.

Both of these scenes, however, are superseded by a memory with an altogether different vibe. That, of course, is crossing the finish line and exchanging a flurry of high-fives and hugs with a bunch of random sweaty strangers, all of us clad in wetsuits, goggles, and running shoes.

You see, I had a blast racing my first Ötillö Swimrun race despite the dead-tired arms and cactus butt.

If you have never heard of the swimrun racing format, here’s a quick primer. Picture a triathlon, minus the biking. Now, chop up the swimming and running portions, stitch them together in smaller portions, and spread the whole event out on a point-to-point course. You run, then swim, then run again, then swim, and so on. The event I did was a “sprint” distance event, comprised of five swims and six runs spread out across 12 miles of trails and lake.

It took me nearly three hours to complete, and at no point was I sprinting.

Unlike triathlon, where you abandon your gear after each portion, swimrun requires you to carry all of your stuff from start to finish. Thus, you must swim while wearing your running shoes, run while clad in your wetsuit, and carry your pull buoy, hand paddles — swimming gear that is allowed — for the entire journey. This makes for some hilarious blunders along the way (more on this later).

Within the swimrun world, Ötillö is the proverbial Ironman — the most recognizable brand of events. Outside has a somewhat rich history of chronicling the Swedish company, first in 2013, then in 2014, and also in a 2017 Brad Stulberg column. In 2019, longtime contributor W. Hodding Carter wrote an Outside feature story about his foibles at the Ötillö world series race in Cannes, France, where he and his partner paddled across the green-blue Mediterranean and jogged through the French Riviera.

In all of those stories, Ötillö swimrun races come across as grueling, fun, and distinctly European. The racing format, after all, was developed in Sweden and first held on the chain of islands just east of Stockholm, which is still the site of the annual Ötillö world championships. The name “Ötillö” is a Swedish word that loosely translates to “island to island.”

Good news for Americans: Ötillö is no longer just for the Euros. In 2023, the series expanded to North America after it purchased a budding collection of U.S. swimrun races called the Odyssey series, that were co-founded by a guy named Lars Finanger. Finanger and I were roommates in Boulder 20 years ago, back when we were both dirtbag triathletes chasing a daily endorphin high.

Now, Finanger is trying to spread the Swedish swimrun gospel in the U.S., where jogging trails while wearing a wetsuit is about as popular as pickled herring.

“We started out with a lot of triathletes, Ironman finishers, Eco-Challenge racers — it was a really eclectic group of endurance athletes,” Finanger told me. “Now we have a small but dedicated following of athletes who see themselves as Swimrunners first, even though they might do a triathlon or a bike race, too.”

Finanger first learned about Ötillö from the 2013 Outside story. He was burned out on triathlon and road bike racing and was looking for a new challenge, so he signed up for the world championship event in Stockholm, which is comprised of 38 miles of running and 5.7 miles of swimming, and requires participants to compete in teams of two. It’s a grueling test of endurance and grit that takes many teams upwards of 10 hours to complete.

“I had this big grin on my face throughout the whole thing, even though the water was so frickin’ cold and the trails made you feel like you were running through the hobbit scene from Lord of the Rings,” Finanger told me. “I realized we didn’t have anything like it in the USA.”

Finanger wanted to start his own race but didn’t know how. As luck would have it, he wasn’t the only person intrigued by the format. Jeffrey Cole, a veteran of the endurance sports industry and a longtime triathlon race director, emailed Finanger about the swimrun format. Cole said that Casco Bay, Maine, near his home in Kennebunkport, was a perfect place to recreate the island hopping of Sweden’s Ötillö. In 2016, they started the inaugural Odyssey event along the Maine coast.

“I think about the history of triathlon, where athletes raced in Kona and then went back home to put on their own races where they lived,” Finanger said. “We wanted to produce a swimrun that we’d have wanted to do ourselves.”

Their model was a success. Finanger and Cole started other swimrun races in the U.S.: Orcas Island, Washington; Cedarville, Michigan; Austin, Texas; and even one on California’s Catalina Island. These events are held annually, and the participation numbers now surpass 400 at some races.

Cole died in 2018, and Finanger kept the business going alongside a handful of new partners. In 2023, Ötillö approached them about purchasing the Odyssey series and bringing it under the corporate umbrella. Finanger said it was a no-brainer.

“It meant partnering with the gold standard in our sport,” he said.

These days, the former Odyssey races award points to elite athletes that help them qualify for the world championships race in Stockholm. But they also boast shorter distances, solo categories, and a laid-back vibe. Because the purpose of the events, Finanger told me, is to attract newbies like yours truly to the format.

“We are still this meeting ground for all of these different types of athletes — swimmers, cyclists, triathletes,” he said. “The one they have in common is they are adventure-minded.”

Qualifying for a race in Europe was not on my mind as I prepared for the 2026 Colorado Ötillö. The shorter sprint distance did not offer qualification points toward the Ötillö World Championship; however, the much longer World Series race in Colorado (23 total miles) did.

When I asked Finanger for strategic advice, he just laughed me off. “Just have fun out there, dude,” he said. He reminded me that the whole point was to have a personal adventure while swimming and jogging my way around the lake.

The laid-back atmosphere at the start line reinforced Finanger’s advice. Over the years, I’ve nervously waited for the start of Ironman triathlons, marathons, and almost every type of bike race out there. At Ötillö, the vibe was extremely chill — like what you’d expect at the start of a 5K color run or a boozy bicycle parade and not a three- to five-hour test of stamina.

Still, I had to remind myself to have fun more than a few times during the early moments of the race. Following a fast one-mile run to start the race, we plunged into Horsetooth Reservoir for the first swim.

I’m a former NCAA Division III swimmer and multiple Ironman finisher, and I’m accustomed to swimming in choppy water filled with thrashing arms and legs. But I struggled to find my groove with the swimrun gear, and I had to stop a few times to position my pull buoy between my legs and learn to swim while wearing sneakers. An even bigger challenge hit when I exited the water.

I stepped onto the clay beach and immediately stumbled around like a newborn fawn. I felt like I’d just gulped a tequila shot or three. I lumbered toward the trail and zigzagged my way up a hill like a punch-drunk boxer.

Upon exiting the water, seasoned swimrunners fastened their pull buoys to their waists with a cord, tucking the apparatus to their lumbar sections like a fanny pack. I fumbled to secure mine as I trotted along, the buoy bouncing off of my butt. As I twisted and twirled the buoy, one of my plastic swim paddles slipped from my hand, and I heard it crash into a bush. Should I stop to look or keep going? I wondered. I chose to stop.

The short pause allowed my thumping heart rate to chill. Soon, my brain fog cleared, and I was able to focus. I found the paddle, and as I jogged along the trail, I familiarized myself with the goofy gear. I practiced tucking and untucking my pull buoy into its tether. I threaded the fingers of my right hand through the elastic loops on my hand paddles to keep them secure.

During a triathlon, you’re constantly using products that are over-engineered for the specific modality of the moment: aerodynamic bike stuff, cushioned shoes, high-visibility swim goggles. Part of the fun quirk of a swimrun is learning to manage the wrong gear when it’s not used for the right job.

My confidence increased, and I picked up the pace, jogging past swimrunners and moving to the side as others jogged past me. People seemed stoked to be on the trail. Nobody seemed so caught up in their own struggles as to skip the customary “Lookin’ good!” or “Go get ’em!” during a pass.

The sprint course deviated from the World Series route near the five-mile mark, and I bid adieu to the athletes who were tackling the longer distance. I saw a handful of sprint racers up ahead of me and decided to push my pace on a long switchback ascent to try and catch them.

Perhaps it was my soaring body temperature inside my wetsuit, or my lingering buzz. But as I closed in on the guy ahead of me, my mind wandered, and I tripped on a rock, completed a somersault, and landed in the cactus. Bewildered, I made a mental note about swimrun: shit can hit the fan if you don’t pay attention.

The fall meant that I had to spend a few minutes plucking spines from my backside once I crossed the line. But the ordeal delivered one of my lasting takeaways from the race.

Perfection does not exist during a swimrun. Even during a shorter distance race, you’re bound to inhale water, drop your gear, battle through exhaustion, or trip and stumble. How you deal with these setbacks defines your experience out there.

I’ve spent the last 25 years trying out different endurance sports. And I’m familiar with the progression that most athletes follow with these sports. You try out a sport and fall in love with the adventure, camaraderie, and community. Then, as the years go by, you focus more on your results, and before you know it, you’re completing a training regimen, following a performance-oriented diet, and dreaming of a top-10 finish.

I will absolutely compete in another Ötillö Swimrun event, but I don’t envision myself ever getting too hardcore about the format. Simply doing a swimrun gave me enough feeling of adventure and carefree silliness, without an ounce of self-seriousness. Sucking at the format provided half of the joy. And I’m more than happy to chase that feeling again.

#8817. A Garden City in the Caribbean: Planning Belize’s New Capital, Belmopan

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

The push for that capital began with a single night of devastation. On October 31, 1961, Hurricane Hattie struck Belize City, the old capital and Caribbean port, destroying roughly 80 percent of its infrastructure and killing nearly 300 people. The extent of the destruction exposed the physical vulnerabilities of maintaining a primary administrative center in a water-surrounded peninsula located at sea level, prompting authorities to re-evaluate the nation's urban future. If British Honduras wanted to enter independence with a capital that could withstand the next storm, it would need to start over somewhere safer. In 1964, the cabinet formally selected an inland site near Roaring Creek Village, located 50 miles west of Belize City, to construct a new capital safe from tropical storm surges and geographically at the center of the new nation of Belize.

Regenerating the City: Changing the Criteria We Build By

Urban designers are being asked to regenerate rather than simply expand, and that means revisiting the criteria used to build and rebuild cities. World Cities Day 2026, observed on October 31 under the theme "Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All," highlighted the United Nations' estimate that up to 3.4 billion people lack adequate housing and approached the challenge through housing, public space, mobility, and neighborhood livability. To improve the urban quality of life to contemporary standards, it's time to change the modern design guidelines that shaped many of our cities, including car-oriented planning. In London, Oxford Street opened its first traffic-free phase, almost a kilometer between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, in a project led by landscape and urban design practice East that adds seating, planting, and places to meet and rest to a historic area long reserved for automobiles.

Projects to Look Forward To: Earth, Reuse, and the Value of the Already Built

Projects of international relevance were announced this week, each one proposing its own connection to heritage and pre-existing structures. In Sharjah, Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha and Daniel Rosselló unveiled the Sharjah Design Centre, due in 2029, which incorporates rammed earth and sits within a research agenda on local and waste-based materials, placing material sustainability at the center of the project. In California, Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD will convert a mid-century warehouse into a museum for the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity, an adaptive reuse initiative that preserves the building's folded concrete roof and industrial imprint. In Milan, Foster + Partners and MANICA revealed the first images of their Generali Stadium, expected to replace San Siro, raising protests and questions. Why does our culture tend to see the new as intrinsically better? Where are we looking for beauty and value?

XIV BIAU Announces Winning Projects and Launches Its Program of Activities in Brasília

The XIV Bienal Iberoamericana de Arquitectura y Urbanismo (Ibero-American Biennial of Architecture and Urbanism, BIAU) opened in Brasília with the inauguration of its exhibition at SESI Lab and the announcement of this edition's winners. Under the theme "Cuidar la Vida" (Caring for Life), the jury recognized twelve projects, six in the Works category and six in Publications, along with five honorable mentions in Obras. The selected designs include a park in Brazil, a floating cinema in Perú, a rural development center in Ecuador, a theater in Chile, and social housing in Spain and Paraguay. Awarded publications explore themes such as the role of architecture in education, historical memory, urban transformation, and environmental challenges. All of the awarded works place care for people and territory at the center of architectural practice, addressing the integration of vegetation and water into built spaces, community life, and access to housing. The Biennial, promoted by Spain's Ministry of Housing and Urban Agenda (MIVAU), continues through November 6 with exhibitions, lectures, debates, and thematic tours across the city.

SOM Unveils Masterplan for a New Coastal City in Egypt

The first phase of Alam Al Roum, a new coastal city masterplan by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, is planned across approximately 4 million square meters, with delivery scheduled to begin in 2030. The initial development will include 2 kilometers of beachfront and promenade, open-sea-connected lagoons, residential and hospitality projects, a town-center marina, and retail and dining areas. The larger 20.6-million-square-meter masterplan envisions a year-round coastal destination organized around interconnected residential, mixed-use, hospitality, education, and business districts. Extending across 7.2 kilometers of coastline, the city is structured around seawater-connected lagoons, which extend the waterfront inland while contributing to stormwater management. Walking paths and trails connect shaded streets, gardens, promenades, and public spaces, complemented by cycling routes and planned transit connections. The masterplan also incorporates climate-responsive design, renewable energy generation, wetlands, stabilized dunes, and a living shoreline to address the site's environmental conditions and changing coastal dynamics.

#8811. Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 Announces Opening Programme Featuring Performances, Films, and Conference

The Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has announced the opening programme of its third edition, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures. Curated by writer and anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, with Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the Triennial will take place from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, with its six-day opening programme running from November 14 to 19. Co-curated by Rao and Sharmeen Inayat, SAT's Research and Civic Engagement Curator, the programme brings together participatory projects, live performances, film screenings, lectures, and discussions across the Emirate of Sharjah, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19.

The Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has announced the opening programme of its third edition, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures. Curated by writer and anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, with Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the Triennial will take place from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, with its six-day opening programme running from November 14 to 19. Co-curated by Rao and Sharmeen Inayat, SAT's Research and Civic Engagement Curator, the programme brings together participatory projects, live performances, film screenings, lectures, and discussions across the Emirate of Sharjah, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19.

The third edition brings together 35 participants whose multidisciplinary practices examine architecture through the relationships, knowledge, and forms of exchange that shape collective life. Events will take place across several locations, including Al Qasimiyah School, Al Jubail Vegetable Market, Al Madam Buried Village, and the Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilization. Throughout the opening week, participant-led tours and live interventions will engage visitors with the Triennial's installations and research, including Tumblespace (or What Binds Us?) by Aslıhan Demirtaş, Ali Cindoruk, and Dilşad Aladağ. The nomadic structure explores connections between people, movement, and place through temporary spaces for gathering and exchange. Badriyah Alsalem will also present The Houses of the Moon and Names of the Sun, performance lectures drawing on observation, poetry, and cultural astronomy to examine relationships between landscape, time, and the sky.

The programme will also include performances exploring the relationship between sound, movement, and spatial experience. Pakistani-American singer Ali Sethi will present BORROWED TIME: trails and tentacles in popular music, while choreographer Omar Rajeh's Origami Bodies will be presented in dialogue with Ziad Jamaleddine's SAT project Lalla Alwyia, Khalwa. The collaboration brings together movement informed by maqam, a practice of instantaneous composition, and a reinterpretation of the khalwa, a secluded space traditionally associated with Sufi retreat and meditation.

Bringing together international scholars, architects, artists, and researchers, the conference will examine how knowledge about cities and regions is produced and how local histories and experiences challenge dominant narratives of urban development. Its panels will address ecological and temporal negotiations in architecture, everyday urban planning, and the institutions and collective practices that emerge following rupture and displacement. Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Let's make this concrete. It's late September — shoulder season, the absolute sweet spot for Ireland travel — and you and your partner want a 10-day trip to explore the Ring of Kerry and the Cliffs of Moher.

The Cash Reality: A round trip from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus in late September runs approximately $550–$650 per person in economy. For two people, you're looking at $1,100–$1,300 before you've spent a single euro in Ireland. That's real money.

The Avios Reality: 13,000 Avios per person, per direction. Round trip for two:

The CPP Math: At a midpoint cash value of $600 per ticket one-way, you're getting 4.6 cents per Avios — nearly triple what most travel rewards programs consider excellent value. Even at the conservative end ($300/ticket), you're at 2.3 cents per point, still well above average.

What the Experience Looks Like: Aer Lingus operates the BOS–DUB route on the Airbus A321LR — a purpose-built transatlantic narrowbody with a dedicated economy cabin, pull-out meal trays, and proper overhead bin space. The overnight flight departs Boston in the evening and arrives Dublin mid-morning, giving you a full day upon arrival. The crew is warm, the food is solid for economy, and there's no connection in London or Amsterdam burning hours off your vacation.

You land at Dublin Airport refreshed (enough), clear customs quickly through the U.S. preclearance facility — one of only a handful in the world — and you're on the road toward Killarney by noon. Your entire transatlantic crossing cost you about 26,000 Avios and $25 in taxes. The Chase Sapphire Preferred welcome bonus alone is worth 60,000 Ultimate Rewards points. This trip is already nearly free before you've optimized anything else.

Amex Membership Rewards periodically runs a 30% transfer bonus to British Airways Avios. When this promotion is live, your 13,000 Avios only costs you approximately 10,000 Amex points. For a family of four round trip (104,000 Avios), that drops to roughly 80,000 Amex points. Set a Google alert for "Amex British Airways transfer bonus" and strike when it appears — these promotions are time-limited.

BA's award search opens 355 days in advance. If you're targeting travel in late spring (May–early June) before peak summer pricing kicks in, mark your calendar and search the moment the window opens. Award space on direct transatlantic routes gets snapped up quickly at good dates.

BA Avios allows open jaw bookings — meaning you can fly into one airport and return from another at the same Avios price. Book Boston → Dublin inbound and Shannon or Cork → Boston outbound, and now your itinerary naturally flows west to east across the country without backtracking. This is the smart traveler's move and it costs you nothing extra in Avios.

British Airways operates some transatlantic routes with a connection through London Heathrow. The moment you're on BA-operated metal, fuel surcharges of $300–$800+ get added to your booking, completely obliterating the value. Always confirm you're booking Aer Lingus flights (flight numbers beginning with EI) when using this strategy.

Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you've transferred points and haven't yet booked, make sure your BA Executive Club account sees some activity within that window. Even earning a few Avios through a BA partner (a hotel stay, a car rental, a shopping portal purchase) resets the clock.

For earning the Avios you need for this redemption, the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (transferring Chase UR to BA at 1:1) or any Amex Membership Rewards card give you the most flexibility. Both transfer instantly to BA. If you're starting from zero, a single card welcome bonus of 60,000–100,000 points covers a round trip for one to three people depending on timing.

Nonstop to Ireland for a fraction of the cash price

Aer Lingus joined the Oneworld alliance, which means British Airways Avios can book Aer Lingus-operated flights. Because BA uses distance-based pricing, the relatively short transatlantic crossing from the East Coast to Dublin (roughly 3,000-3,500 miles) prices at just 13,000 Avios each way in economy. Compare this to using American Airlines miles (30,000+ each way) or other programs for the same transatlantic flight. The distance-based chart rewards this specific geography with disproportionately low pricing, creating one of the best-value transatlantic sweet spots available.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Verify that Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from your departure city to Dublin. The strongest year-round service is from Boston and New York. Seasonal routes may only operate during summer months.

Log into your British Airways Executive Club account and search for flights from your city to Dublin using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for Aer Lingus-operated flights (flight numbers starting with EI). Check flexible dates for the best availability.

Once you find availability, transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant from Chase and Amex.

Complete the booking on ba.com. The total will show 13,000 Avios plus taxes and surcharges (typically $50-$100 each way). Review the total out-of-pocket before confirming to make sure it meets your value threshold.

Add your Aer Lingus or Oneworld frequent flyer number to earn status credits. Remember that Dublin offers U.S. Preclearance for return flights — a significant time-saver. Consider booking accommodations using hotel points for a fully points-funded trip.

Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from Boston (BOS), New York (JFK), Newark (EWR), Hartford (BDL), Philadelphia (PHL), Washington Dulles (IAD), Chicago (ORD), and other seasonal routes. Boston and New York have the most frequent service year-round.

Aer Lingus awards do carry fuel surcharges, typically $100-$200 round trip in economy. While not zero, this is still dramatically less than the $500-$1,000+ cash fare. The net savings remain substantial despite the surcharges.

Dublin can serve as an excellent gateway to the rest of Europe. Aer Lingus offers connections to many European cities from Dublin, and you can also book separate budget airline flights within Europe. Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: New members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

The BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.

#8808. What AI Reveals About Architecture That Was Never Built

Some architectural projects only survive as drawings, competition entries, or models in archives. Others were built, but not as first imagined, and the completed building gradually replaced the original proposal in collective memory. Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral is familiar to many, but less well known is his Warrant Design, the spire-topped proposal approved in 1675 that he subsequently reworked as construction progressed. London was also once offered a very different monument: Thomas Willson's vast pyramid-shaped necropolis for Primrose Hill, designed to accommodate millions of burials and dominate the city's skyline.

Some architectural projects only survive as drawings, competition entries, or models in archives. Others were built, but not as first imagined, and the completed building gradually replaced the original proposal in collective memory. Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral is familiar to many, but less well known is his Warrant Design, the spire-topped proposal approved in 1675 that he subsequently reworked as construction progressed. London was also once offered a very different monument: Thomas Willson's vast pyramid-shaped necropolis for Primrose Hill, designed to accommodate millions of burials and dominate the city's skyline.

These projects have outlived the circumstances that prevented their realization, whether financial, political, or technical. Some addressed practical needs through extraordinary forms; others explored how infrastructure, buildings, and cities could support new ways of living. New visualization technologies offer ways to revisit these works and examine ideas that, in some cases, anticipated the scale and complexity of contemporary megaprojects. A series being developed by Gendo explores this possibility through historical proposals that were never built or underwent significant changes before completion. Using archival drawings, models, and descriptions as starting points, it considers how generative tools might bring these ideas into view for contemporary audiences, while making clear where documentation ends and interpretation begins.

Among the earlier proposals is Charles-François Ribart de Chamoust's colossal triumphal elephant for the Champs-Élysées, conceived in 1758 with elaborate interiors, including a dining room with trees and a stream. A later elephant monument proposed under Napoleon for the Place de la Bastille reached the stage of a full-scale plaster model, which remained on the site for decades. Claude-Nicolas Ledoux's work similarly extended beyond his built tollhouses for Paris to more unusual proposals, including classical structures on boats intended to collect tolls from river traders. In his cenotaph for Isaac Newton, Étienne-Louis Boullée imagined a monumental sphere whose interior would evoke the night sky.

In his cenotaph for Isaac Newton, Étienne-Louis Boullée imagined a monumental sphere whose interior would evoke the night sky.

Early twentieth-century proposals explored the possibilities of new materials, infrastructure, and urban organization. Antonio Sant'Elia's Città Nuova imagined a layered city of elevators, bridges, and power stations, with a visual language that invites comparison with the later worlds of Metropolis and Blade Runner. Mies van der Rohe's Friedrichstraße skyscraper explored the architectural potential of a glass envelope, while Erich Mendelsohn's sketches and Hermann Finsterlin's proposals pursued expressive, almost biological forms.

Mies van der Rohe's Friedrichstraße skyscraper explored the architectural potential of a glass envelope, while Erich Mendelsohn's sketches and Hermann Finsterlin's proposals pursued expressive, almost biological forms.

Other projects challenged architectural conventions more directly. Adolf Loos, known for his criticism of ornament, entered the Chicago Tribune competition with a skyscraper shaped like a giant Doric column. The Hotel Attraction, a soaring tower proposed for Lower Manhattan and attributed to Antoni Gaudí, introduces a different question: how to interpret a project whose authorship and surviving drawings remain subjects of debate.

Postwar proposals expanded these ambitions to entire urban systems. Arata Isozaki's Clusters in the Air organized spaces around tree-like structural cores above Tokyo. Ron Herron's Walking City for Archigram imagined mobile structures crossing landscapes on telescopic legs. Rem Koolhaas's Bangkok Hyperbuilding proposed concentrating an entire urban environment within a single structure. Some of these projects were intended to be built on specific sites and others used drawings and models to explore ideas about architecture and urban life without aiming for construction.

Architectural visualization combines technical skill with decisions about composition, materials, lighting, context, and occupation. A photorealistic image can make a proposal immediately legible to viewers unfamiliar with architectural drawings. Producing such images has traditionally required considerable time and specialized expertise.

A photorealistic image can make a proposal immediately legible to viewers unfamiliar with architectural drawings. Producing such images has traditionally required considerable time and specialized expertise.

The choice of medium also affects what an image communicates. A watercolor can suggest atmosphere while leaving details unresolved. A section can explain spatial relationships without describing every surface. Photorealism gives those surfaces and details greater apparent certainty, which can be useful when presenting a developed proposal but misleading when decisions are still provisional.

Historical architects worked with the representational tools available to them. Their drawings and models could communicate powerful visions, yet translating those visions for patrons, committees, or the public remained a challenge. The ability to make an unfamiliar idea understandable can influence whether it gains support, alongside questions of cost, feasibility, and political will.

Historical architects worked with the representational tools available to them. Their drawings and models could communicate powerful visions, yet translating those visions for patrons, committees, or the public remained a challenge. The ability to make an unfamiliar idea understandable can influence whether it gains support, alongside questions of cost, feasibility, and political will.

Generative visualization tools allow architects to turn an initial concept into an image more quickly and test different materials, lighting conditions, and viewpoints. Architects still need to decide what the image should communicate and which details to include. When revisiting historical projects, some of those details may be missing from the original drawings and choosing a facade material or placing people around a building can make its appearance and scale easier to understand, but these additions reflect decisions made today.

The Gendo series distinguishes between three approaches: evidence-based visualization, grounded interpretation, and open-ended provocation. Each image is intended to be labeled according to its relationship with the original documentation.

At the evidence-based end, the proposed visualization of Willson's pyramid uses survey data and defined camera positions to place the structure within aerial views of Primrose Hill and the wider London skyline. Drawing on methods used for verified views in planning applications, the exercise aims to test technical accuracy as well as visual persuasion. Mies's Friedrichstraße tower receives similar treatment within its Berlin site, while Wren's Warrant Design will be shown alongside the cathedral that was built, allowing direct comparison.

The rigor of these images depends on the underlying geometry, site information, and production process. Grounded interpretation allows more room for decisions where the historical record is incomplete. Original drawings, descriptions, and photographs of models guide the work, while lighting, materials, and surroundings give the proposals a more tangible presence. The Hotel Attraction in Lower Manhattan, Boullée's cenotaph on a plausible French site, and Isozaki's clusters reconstructed from photographs of his models fall within this approach.

Open-ended provocation deliberately moves further from literal reconstruction. Finsterlin's and Mendelsohn's expressive forms can become starting points for experiments that follow the spirit of their work, potentially in dialogue with the visual worlds of H. R. Giger or M. C. Escher. Loos's column-shaped tower invites another kind of response: covering it in graffiti and tattoos would revisit the architect's own associations between ornament and bodily decoration. None of these images constitutes a definitive completion of another architect's work. Their labels help explain how much rests on historical evidence and how much comes from contemporary imagination.

The series also places historical proposals in dialogue with later projects and visual cultures. Boullée's cenotaph, for example, can be considered alongside the LED-covered Sphere proposed for Stratford in London, a counterpart to the venue in Las Vegas that was refused planning permission in 2023. Although radically different in purpose, the two spherical monuments invite a comparison of what different periods choose to monumentalize: scientific understanding and the cosmos in one case, entertainment in the other.
