#8727. Replacing Your Bike Chain Is Easier Than You Think—Here’s How to Do It at Home

A step-by-step home repair guide to measuring, removing, and installing a bike chain.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Replacing a chain is a great way for someone to tap into their home bike maintenance potential. It’s a pretty straightforward process once you’re used to it, especially if you have the existing chain to measure from. I typically recommend being familiar with a few skills before diving into replacing your chain. The first skill to know is adjusting your front and rear derailleurs. The second is knowing how to use a chain checker. The third is being familiar with a pre bike check. This last one is especially helpful because it will allow you to run through the bike to see if there are any other issues before diving into swapping out your chain. Again, these skills are not required skills to replace a chain, but having some familiarity with the basic mechanics addressed above will only help make this process easier. Here we’ll go through the tools you’ll need and the basic process to replace your chain at home.

How often should you replace your chain? Before answering that question, it helps to understand the process of chain wear. As your chain ages, each link’s internal bushings slowly lengthen. In turn, your now-longer chain puts added pressure on your cassette cogs and chainring teeth, causing them to wear faster. This also hampers shifting quality.

To avoid this accelerated wear of your cassette and chainrings, a general rule of thumb is to replace your bike’s chain every 2,000 miles. Mind you, this is just a starting point. No two chains will wear at exactly the same rate because no two riders treat their chains the same.

These differences in riding style are why it is best to periodically use a chain wear measuring tool to determine the condition of your chain. With the tool in hand, apply pressure to a pedal so the top of the chain is taut, and then place the measuring tool in place on the chain as shown in the video above and read the results. Indicators on the tool will tell you whether it’s time to replace your chain.

Cutting a new bike chain to the correct length for installation and removing a damaged link for an on-trail chain repair are essentially the same job. Make life easier by using a full-size tool at home, and save the compact tool for midride fixes.

To start, you’ll need to pick up the right size chain for your bike. We’re not talking about the length of the chain here (you’ll address that later), but width. This is dictated by the number of cogs on your cassette; a six-speed bike uses the same width chain as an eight-speed, but a nine-speed needs something different, and so on. (Check out Park Tool’s chain compatibility guide for more on this.) The easiest way to ensure you get the right chain is to buy the same kind of chain that came on your bike. If you decide to go with a different chain, it’s best to get one from the same manufacturer.

If your chain has a master link such as a Shimano Quick Link or SRAM PowerLock, use a pair of master link pliers to compress the link and undo it. (If it’s a newer chain, you might be able to do this with your hands.)

If there isn’t a master link, remove the chain using the chain breaker tool. Back out the tool’s pin to make room and fit a chain link into the outer slot, and line up the tool’s pin with a pin on the chain. Tighten the tool until its pin puts light pressure on the chain’s connecting pin. Crank the handle, making sure the tool’s pin stays straight. If it twists, stop and realign everything so as not to bend the tool’s pin. If you bend it, most tools have replaceable pins available; some even come with one inside the handle. Then push the pin far enough through so you can remove the extra links.

Remove the chain from your bike. Then, measure out the length of your new chain to match the length of your old chain, taking into account the master link. Remove any excess links from the new chain using the chain breaker tool, and install the master link. Thread the new chain onto your bike’s cassette and chainring and connect the ends with the master link, making sure the link is secure and locked in place.

When she’s not out riding her mountain bike, Jessica is an editor for Popular Mechanics. She was previously an editor for Bicycling magazine.

#8726. Locust Pose Might Be a Simple Backbend, But It Can Help Improve Your Posture

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the backbend Locust Pose first appeared in the July-August 1996 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

If a picture is worth a thousand words, then our posture speaks volumes. Poor carriage of the torso—rounded shoulders, sunken chest, and a downward cast of the eyes—generally suggests a negative state of being. Good posture, on the other hand—shoulders rolled back and down, chest lifted, and an energetic carriage—demonstrates confidence and a sense of purpose.

All the backbending yoga postures help create this physical expression of assurance. You feel better, have more energy, and benefit from an enhanced respiratory system. The internal alignment of the organs is refined as we adjust and improve the external alignment.

The postures actually have the potential to positively and profoundly affect you on all levels: physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual. Approaching your asanas with this awareness is the key to the enrichment of your practice.

The repertoire of backbending postures, or hyperextensions of the spine, is vast. In this article, we are going to focus on one of the more basic back-bending poses, Grasshopper or Locust Pose (Salabhasana). There are several variations of this posture, according to different systems or styles of hatha yoga. We will practice two versions of Locust, beginning with Salabhasana One as described in B.K.S. Iyengar’s Light on Yoga.

Locust is excellent for correcting poor posture, as well as for counteracting the development of kyphosis, the rounding of the upper back. It tones the whole posterior of the body, strengthens the abdominals, and enhances digestion.

Begin by lying face down on your mat, with your arms at your sides near your hips, palms facing upward. Tuck your chin in, forehead on the floor.

Engage your abdominals by drawing your navel in and up, to stabilize your lower back. Contract your buttocks and quadriceps. Keep the knees, legs, and feet together. Exhale the breath as you simultaneously raise the head, chest, arms, and legs. Look forward and up. Hold and breathe for five to 10 seconds. Keep the abdominals firm so you feel the support from underneath.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position. Turn your head to the side and completely relax. Repeat once or twice more.

Full Locust begins in the same base position, but with the arms outstretched at shoulder level, perpendicular to the body. The palms are facing down, and the chin is on the mat. The knees, legs, and feet are together.

Engage your abdominal muscles by drawing your navel in and up; contract your buttocks and quadriceps. This time, inhale the breath as you raise the arms, chest, head, and legs. Look forward and up. Breathe naturally as you hold the posture for five to 10 seconds. Keep your shoulders away from your earlobes as you continue to stretch your arms back and slightly upward. Palms remain facing the floor. The idea is to lift the entire body upward as you balance on the center of your abdomen.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position, and relax. Repeat once or twice more.

If your lower back is sensitive or you are prone to chronic neck tension, you may want to practice the pose in the following stages.

Lie on your stomach, face down, arms at your sides near your hips. Palms are facing up, the chin is tucked in, and the forehead is on the floor. Legs are hip-distance apart. Firm the buttocks and abdominals as well as the quadriceps.

Inhale the breath. Exhaling, raise just the arms to about hip level, keeping the palms facing up. The head remains on the floor. Lengthen the neck and focus on strengthening your back muscles. Feel your shoulder blades pull down your back and slightly together.

Keep the abdominals, buttocks, and legs firm. Exhale and lower down.

Next, repeat what you’ve just done and add the lifting of the chest. The neck and head will come up as well, but keep looking downward so the neck remains extended rather than arched. Inhale in your base position. Exhale and raise the arms only. Inhale and hold. Ex-haling, raise the chest. Again, hold and breathe rhythmically for five to 10 seconds. Exhale as you lower down.

In the same beginning position, inhale the breath, and exhale raising the arms up. Hold and inhale. Exhale, raising the chest. Hold and inhale. Finally, exhale and raise the legs. Hold and breathe. Keep looking at the floor, focusing on lengthening the body from the top of your head to your fingertips on down to your toes. When you’re ready, lower down on an exhalation. Turn your head to the side, release the pose completely, and relax.

A natural inclination after performing a back bend is to pull your knees to your chest. So after your last repetition, you may want to got into Child’s Pose: Kneel back onto your heels, folding your torso over your thighs with your head resting on the floor in front of your knees. Arms are at your sides with palms facing up.

If your head doesn’t rest on the floor easily, simply fold your arms underneath your forehead for support.

#8725. How to Diagnose and Fix These Common Bike Noises, Including Pedal Clicking

A bike that squeaks, rattles, and clicks is annoying and frustrating. Use these tips to troubleshoot the most common and mysterious bike sounds.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. So first, you’ll need to know how to diagnose it.

The most common noise makers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Below are the most common culprits of pesky bike noises, including bike pedal clicking. Use these suggestions to help you narrow down and silence them. If you lack the proper tools to fix an issue (or fear a fix is above your skill level), seek assistance from your local bike shop or a trusted bicycle mechanic.

That creaky squeaking you hear as you pedal might mean that your bike’s chain needs lube. Cleaning and lubing your chain is usually a good place to start with any weird noise, but if it doesn’t solve the squeak, you may need to do other drivetrain maintenance or replace the chain.

Your chain should also be the first thing you check if you hear a rattling sound while riding. It could mean the loose, excess chain is contacting your frame (this is commonly called “chain slap”). It can also mean your derailleur is out of adjustment and not shifting properly.

A worn chain can also cause noise. Bicycle chains wear out with use as the bushings and rollers in the chain become worn down by grit and grime. This causes slop to develop and the distance between the pin centers to increase. (This is commonly called “chain stretch,” though the metal in the chain hasn’t actually stretched.)

Generally, when a chain “stretches” by 0.5 percent, it is time to change it. If you ride a lot, a chain checker is handy for knowing when it’s time to replace your chain.

Pro Tip: You can also use a ruler to check chain wear. A fresh chain measures 12 inches from pin center to pin center. If it measures more than 12-¹⁄₁₆ inches, change your chain.

If you notice a noise with every pedal stroke, it might be the pedals themselves. To remedy this, remove your pedals, grease the threads, and reinstall them on your bike (remember, both pedals tighten to the front of the bike). When installing, replace the washers (if any) between the pedal and crank arm.

Another source of squeaks might be your shoes’ cleats. Check that your cleats are tight—a loose cleat bolt can cause headaches. While checking the bolts, check for excess wear. Sometimes, the sounds are a sign that the cleats need replacement. An occasional drop or two of wax-based lubricant on two-bolt cleats can help keep the squeaks at bay.

Pro Tip: If your cleats and pedals get squeaky during a ride, a quick squirt of energy drink or something sugary like Gatorade can sometimes quiet them down until you get home and apply lube.

If your bike has internal cable routing, a rattling noise emanating from inside your frame when going over bumps (or knocking when turning) is commonly caused by derailleur housing or hydraulic brake lines. While the sound is rarely cause for concern, it drives riders crazy and can take you out of the zone when training.

Unfortunately, the fix for this issue isn’t usually quick or easy and requires some advanced mechanic skills (especially if dealing with hydraulic brakes). On some bikes—like Trek’s Boone, which has a port on the downtube for this purpose—it could be as simple as adding a zip tie to hold the cables. Other bikes might require the disassembly of the brake hoses and shifter housing (and even the stem and headset on some bikes) to apply sound-damping foam tubing to the lines.

Thankfully, the fix is much easier on bikes with externally routed cables and hoses that have rattling cables. This noise is usually caused when the housing slaps together over bumps on the trail or rough road surfaces. Some pro mechanics heat-shrink the housing together to prevent the sound, but electrical tape can also be used. Another solution is cable clips that keep the housing and hoses from contacting.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM Dub and RaceFace Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

Not long ago, disc brakes were almost only found on high-end bikes and mountain bikes. However, these powerful stoppers are now common on almost all genres of bikes and at all price levels. And disc brakes make some unique sounds that can drive cyclists bonkers.

A chattering sound coming from your rotors might indicate a loose rotor. Check that the rotor bolts or lockring are sufficiently tight. Most disc brakes with 6-bolt rotors use a T25 Torx to tighten. For Centerlock rotors, a cassette lockring tool is used for internal-style lockrings. For external-type lockrings, a rotor/external BB wrench is used.

If your disc brakes are squealing and screeching when you apply the brakes, the brake pads or rotors may be contaminated. This commonly happens from oil residue thrown up from the road when you ride in the rain, contamination from aerosol lubricants, or any one of dozens of other causes.

If the contamination is not too bad, it can often be cleaned off. To do this, remove the wheel and thoroughly wipe down the disc rotor and pads with a clean shop rag or towel and isopropyl alcohol. If you notice significant discoloration of the rotor or grooves in the pads, either or both may need replacement. Your local bike shop can help get you the correct replacement pads and rotors for your brake system.

Pro Tip: If you swap wheelsets on your bike for different rides or races, recenter the disc brake caliper each time you change the wheel. It takes a few extra minutes but helps ensure brake pads wear evenly and reduces rotor rub.

The occasional zing and ting from disc rotors are normal, and these sounds often come and go during a ride as the rotors heat up under hard braking and cool down afterward. If you hear a continuous pinging noise from the rotors, your rotors might need straightening. Head to the below story for more detailed info on diagnosing and fixing common disc brake issues.

A loose headset usually makes a rattling or thunking sound. And a headset that’s too loose can make your bike handle poorly or even damage your frame or fork beyond repair. To tighten a threadless headset system, loosen the bolts on the side of your stem, then tighten the top cap bolt. Tight the bolt enough to pull the fork, headset, stem, and any headset spacers snugly together (but not so tight that the bars can’t turn freely).

After everything is snug and turns smoothly without play in the bearings, retighten the stem bolts. Use a torque wrench to bring the stem to the manufacturer’s recommended spec (this is sometimes noted on the stem in N/m). Because you have the torque wrench out, this is also a good time to check that your stem’s faceplate bolts are sufficiently tight.

If the rattling doesn’t go away after tightening the headset, take your bike to the shop to be safe. Sometimes, the headset might need a shim spacer—but it’s important to check that it’s not a problem with your fork or steerer tube.

Another common source of creaking is your seatpost—particularly if it occurs only while seated. To fix it, remove your seatpost by undoing the quick release (if there is one) or loosening the hex bolt at its base where it enters the frame.

Pro Tip: Before removing your post, measure the seat height (from the center of the crank bolt to the top of the saddle) with a tape measure. Or, mark the position with electrical tape on the seatpost where it meets the seat clamp or frame.

After removing the post, wipe off any grit on the seatpost and inside the seat tube with a rag, and apply a thin layer of grease or fiber grip compound (if you have a carbon frame or are using a carbon post) inside the seat tube. Finally, reinstall the post, tighten the binder bolt to the correct torque, and check if the post still creaks.

If the post still creaks after applying grease and retightening the binder, the noise might be coming from the head of the post or the saddle rails. To check this, undo the hardware that clamps the saddle and the seat from the post. Then, wipe down the hardware and saddle rails with a rag to remove any grit or grime that built up. Finally, reinstall the seat and hardware and tighten them to the manufacturer’s recommended torque.

Chainrings are noise makers when they loosen up and are often overlooked by riders. And if your bike has replaceable rings (with bolts versus riveted together), tightening chainring bolts is an easy fix.

Use the correct side hex or Torx wrench (often 5mm to T30) to the proper torque value. To help prevent the chainring bolts from coming loose again, apply some thread lock compound to the threads.

Pro Tip: Many chainring bolts use a slotted nut on the backside of the ring. If your chainring bolt spins and will not tighten, use a chainring nut tool to hold the nut while tightening the bolt.

If you hear a constant clicking (especially in certain gears) while pedaling, it might mean a shift cable is stretched. (This cable “stretch” is usually the cable housing and ferrules compressing). Cable stretch requires derailleur adjustment for the chain to sit correctly on the gears and not rub the derailleur cage.

First, ensure the derailleur is aligned and the hanger isn’t bent (see below). Then, adjust the cable tension using the barrel adjuster (usually on the rear derailleur on road or gravel bikes and the shifter for mountain bikes). If this doesn’t solve the clicking, you might need to replace your shifter cable and housing.

A bent or misaligned derailleur hanger can cause a constant clicking sound while pedaling. This part (which connects your rear derailleur to the frame) can bend in a crash or incident. They are often replaceable and cheaper to replace than an entire frame.

A bent derailleur hanger might be easy to spot. However, sometimes, a slight bend can cause clicking and poor shifting. (This is especially true for 12-speed drivetrains where even the slightest bend can cause the chain to skip.) If the derailleur hanger isn’t cracked or bent too far to be saved, a hanger alignment tool can be used to straighten it out.

Sometimes, creaking occurs from the derailleur hanger rubbing against the frame where it’s mounted. To remedy this, remove the derailleur hanger, thoroughly clean the frame and hanger, and apply some anti-seize paste to the surfaces that touch.

Pro Tip: Derailleur hangers always seem to break at inopportune moments (like the night before an important race or a holiday when shops are closed). Hangers are relatively low-cost ($25-$50) so, it’s good to have a spare or two in your toolbox. Derailleurhanger.com is a good source for many hangers, especially for older bikes and out-of-business brands.

If you’re purchasing a new bike soon, look for ones using the new Universal Derailleur Hanger standard. Since this hanger is used on many bikes, it’s commonly stocked by many shops. (It also ensures frame compatibility with SRAM’s latest-generation Transmission drivetrains.) Most bikes using UDH are mountain bikes, but it is now popping up on gravel bikes (like the Santa Cruz Stigmata) and road bikes (like the Ritte Esprit).

A noisy thru axle or quick release might need to be tightened. But if tightening it doesn’t quiet the sound, it’s likely one of two problems. A creak or squeak is often a sign of a dry or dirty thru axle or quick release. Remove the thru axle from the frame or fork, clean it, and re-grease it with a thin coat of bike-specific grease. A clicking sound could signify that a thru axle or QR is cracked or broken. This requires immediate replacement.

Pro Tip: If you remove your wheels to get your bike to and from rides, put the thru axles in the frame or fork during transport. This protects your bike from side-load damage and keeps your thru axle from being left behind on your workbench or the trailhead (or getting lost under a car seat).

Far more uncommon than the issues listed above, a cracked or defective frame can be the reason for a persistent, mysterious noise. Frame defects or cracks sometimes aren’t immediately visible and can be hard to diagnose.

Frame damage (from a crash, shipping damage, etc) can also be the culprit. Hairline cracks in carbon frames can be hard to find with the naked eye. When in doubt, bring the bike to an experienced shop for a full inspection. Some companies that repair carbon frames also offer frame inspections. Ruckus Composites in Portland, Oregon, offers ultrasonic inspection to check frames for cracks and damage.

Sometimes, simply thoroughly washing your bike and cleaning and lubing the chain is all it takes to set everything right again. But if you can’t figure out the issue or aren’t sure how to fix it when you do, it’s always a safe bet to take your bike to your local shop or mechanic for service.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8724. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

#8723. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. Inside Italy’s Terra X Cube, a Tour de France simulation became a real-world heat test.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I looked into the giant chamber filled with strategically placed bike trainers and couldn’t help but question what I signed up for. The chamber we were walking into is called the Terra X Cube located in Bolzano, Italy, and is designed to replicate conditions from anywhere on the planet. The chamber can recreate a snowstorm on Mount Everest or a heat wave in the Sahara.

Variables like temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, and altitude can all be controlled from a small observation room just one door over. I knew immediately when I crossed into the threshold of the chamber and the heat hit me in the face that this would be a rough trainer ride.

I was in Bolzano, Italy for an opportunity to participate in this testing in the Terra X Cube as well as tour the apparel brand Q36.5’s headquarters based in Bolzano. The apparel from Q36.5 quickly became my top choice for cycling apparel after getting the chance to test some pieces from their kit for the last few months. Our hot and humid summer in the Northeast gave a perfect testing ground for the Q36.5 Dottore jersey and bibs—and they shined. When a chance to learn more about this brand by visiting their Italian headquarters came up, I jumped on a plane—the opportunity to experience riding in a climate chamber was a special bonus.

Here I’m going to talk about the unique experience of riding in a climate chamber with the heat turned up and my biggest takeaway that you can apply to your trainer riding this season.

The test course and climate were designed to replicate the last section of Stage 2 from the 2026 men’s Tour de France ending in Barcelona. We rode with a custom workout in Zwift and our data was being tracked across the board: SRM cranks to track power, heart rate data to validate fatigue, and CORE sensors to track our heat strain throughout the workout. The room was set to a balmy 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

There was even a tester from Q36.5 in the room with us with a custom jersey. The jersey he wore was effectively two jerseys cut in half at the zipper and straight down the back. He had multiple CORE heat sensors attached around his body to track which jersey design and material was more effective at thermoregulation. One of those jersey designs will end up in a future product.

The ride was supposed to last for about 45 minutes, but our group was the first of the day and ran into some technical difficulties getting the trainers set up. In one sense this was good because we were able to have an extended warmup on the trainers, but the reality meant we spent an extra 45 minutes warming up in the already heated up chamber.

Thankfully, over the last few months, I’ve been doing heat training protocols with my CORE training sensor. I dove straight in with six weeks of active heat training, then I pivoted to strictly passive heat training with my home sauna. While I was absolutely heating up I was relatively comfortable rolling into the ride.

Once we got through our extended warmup we began the proper ride. Effectively we were shooting for an over-under workout that emulated the end of stage two at this year’s Tour de France. I had my CORE temperature data up on the screen and saw that before we were starting the ride my internal temperature was at about 99 degrees. The giant fans at the front of the room would change power to replicate the airflow during climbs versus descents, but at those temperatures it felt like sitting in front of a massive hair dryer.

As we began the official warmup my temperature steadily climbed—according to my CORE sensor I peaked just over 102 degrees. In the middle of the test I looked around the room and everyone looked like they were putting out high effort, even when we were supposed to be sitting in our recovery phase. The heat was taking its toll and our views did not inspire a boost in energy. Staring at the metallic walls while pedaling on our hamster wheel bikes did not give inspiration for an extra push for our final sprint. But as we finished up our not-so-cool cooldown I couldn’t help but think I would do it again.

After our group left the chamber the second group queued up for their turn on the bikes. The technical difficulties were overcome with our group, so they were able to jump straight into the ride after a five-minute warmup. That night we all regrouped to go through the data and we were able to see our data versus the data from some of the professionals in the stage we recreated. My biggest takeaway from the comparison to the professionals was their core temperature data. The professionals we were comparing against showed very little heat strain compared to even the fittest in our group. It’s worth noting the professionals had also already ridden over 60 miles before our route even started—those professionals were extremely heat adapted.

My biggest personal takeaway was how I could recreate this at home. When I talked to someone else in my group we discussed the similarities to this experience and heat training at home. When I do an active heat session at home I layer up in three layers top and bottom, a painter’s suit with the shins and feet cut off (so it doesn’t get caught in the cranks), and a hat or beanie for good measure. My active heat session numbers at home are surprisingly similar to this experience: typically a 45-minute warmup gets me into zone three of the heat strain index in the CORE app and then I spend about 45 minutes in this zone. This shows you don’t need a massive climate chamber to get the training benefits of heat training. Some warm layers, a painter’s suit, a CORE sensor, and a bike trainer can give you the benefits you need to develop this component of training.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8720. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.
